live.name: Commons
live.line: A social platform on one shared, newest-first timeline. Posts, likes, comments, follows.

notes.d: Likes and follows upsert against composite unique constraints, so a double-tap cannot create a duplicate row. The button rolls its optimistic update back if the request fails.
Per-viewer likedByMe resolves inside the same findMany through a filtered relation include, against an explicit descending index on createdAt — no second round trip.
A build-time provisioning script pushes the schema and seeds only when the users table is empty, so anything visitors wrote survives the next deploy.

live.alt: The Commons home page: a dark timeline headed “Everything said here, in the order it was said”, with a sidebar counting 10 people, 24 posts and 89 likes.

live.name: CivicPulse
live.line: Photograph a civic problem; a vision model classifies it, routes it to the department that owns it, and checks the repair photos before it can be closed.

notes.d: Twelve categories are scored from natural-language prompts, with a twenty-prompt distractor bucket for screenshots, pets and clean roads. Fail that or a 0.35 probability floor and the upload comes back 422 rather than being filed wrong.

notes.t: Location from the photo, not the phone
notes.d: A hand-written EXIF parser reads the camera’s own GPS and outranks the browser fix; Tesseract reads street signage in the frame and geocodes it to snap the pin to a real premises.
Perceptual hashes compare every “after” photo against the “before” set. A Hamming distance of five or less is treated as reused evidence and hard-rejects the closure.

live.alt: CivicPulse sign-in page headed “From ‘I reported it’ to ‘We resolved it.’”, with a panel of citizen and municipal-worker demo accounts.

live.name: Transmission
live.line: Real-time chat with friends, end-to-end encrypted private conversations, and voice and video calls.

notes.t: The server stores what it cannot read
notes.d: Private messages are encrypted in the sender’s browser with AES-GCM under ECDH-derived keys and stored as ciphertext. Once a conversation carries an encrypted message, the server refuses plaintext into it, so an old client cannot quietly downgrade it.
Two friends compare a 60-digit safety number. Swap either person’s key and the number changes, which a test asserts.

Voice and video run browser to browser over WebRTC. The server relays only call setup, and that is sealed too, so it can neither read the network details inside nor swap in its own fingerprint to intercept the media. No crypto or WebRTC library is involved: the whole app has four runtime dependencies.
Serverless functions cannot hold a WebSocket open, so Postgres is the fan-out point: each stream tails rows past a BIGSERIAL cursor and hands the browser a resume point before the function times out.

live.alt: Transmission sign-in screen headed “Rooms that stay live”, listing live delivery, end-to-end encrypted private conversations, and encrypted voice and video calls.

links.label: What the encryption does not protect

live.name: Steel Access Doors
live.line: A redesigned website for Steel Access Doors, a clean-room solutions company in Hyderabad, with a 3D model of every product.

notes.d: Each of the 19 products has its own 3D model, built in code to match its product photo, down to the handles and hinges. Visitors can rotate and zoom it, and tap a door or pass box to open it.

notes.t: The home page is a doorway
notes.d: Scrolling swings open a steel double door and carries the camera into a clean room, showing the product in the setting it is made for.
Without WebGL, or if the 3D library cannot load, it falls back to a CSS doorway and product photos, and it respects reduced-motion settings.

live.alt: The Steel Access Doors home page: the company name beside a rendered 3D steel double door, with a prompt to scroll to open it.

live.name: Credential
live.line: An authentication service built around refresh-token theft rather than the usual hash-and-issue demo.
live.note: Refresh tokens are opaque and stored only as digests. Every refresh retires its predecessor inside one transaction; replaying a retired token is read as a copy and revokes the whole rotation family. Access tokens carry a session id that is re-checked on every request, so “sign out everywhere” is immediate rather than waiting out the token lifetime.
live.alt: The Credential authentication demo running in the browser.

live.name: SplitUPI
live.line: Splits group bills, then works out the fewest UPI transfers that clear everyone.
live.note: Greedy matching settles a group but not minimally, so the solver runs a bitmask search for disjoint zero-sum subgroups and settles each pocket on its own — checked against brute force over 381 random ledgers. Money is integer paise throughout, so all six split strategies reconcile to the last paisa. The QR encoder and the UPI deep-link builder are both written from scratch.
live.alt: SplitUPI on its first run, headed “Your shared money, settled.” with a prompt to create a group.

live.name: Smart Dustbin
live.line: Touchless ESP32 bin with a fleet dashboard, plus an in-browser twin of the firmware.
live.note: Rubbish is never flat, so one downward sensor over a peak reads “full” at half empty. Two sensors on opposite diagonals are fused into one figure, flagging an uneven load when they disagree by more than 25 points. From 90% the lid refuses a hand; the only ways past are a safety re-open and the collection crew’s override. The map shows 48 simulated bins across Hyderabad, identical in every browser, with Firestore sharing what visitors and any real board actually did.
live.alt: The Smart Dustbin site, headed “It opens by itself. And it tells the city when it is full.”

live.name: Tally
live.line: Turns a supplier invoice into a picking checklist that staff tick off and photograph, and an admin signs off.
live.note: It reads whatever the supplier sent: a structured model read, then the PDF text layer, then OCR, keeping the best result. A dependency-free parser proves each line by finding quantity × price ≈ amount among its numbers, across US, Indian-lakh and European digit grouping. Every PDF is opened in a short-lived child process with a memory cap, so a hostile file fails one upload rather than the server.
live.alt: The Tally home page: a large TALLY wordmark, admin and staff sign-in panels, and a sample picking checklist with four ticked lines.

live.name: Crumb & Co. strategy
live.line: A six-month digital marketing strategy for a fictional home bakery launching online, built with free tools only.

notes.d: 150 online orders a month within six months, a quarter of them from repeat customers, before any platform is chosen.
Instagram, Google Business Profile and WhatsApp Business, each chosen for how the audience finds and buys. Paid ads are left out because the brief allows only free resources.
Each goal maps to KPIs with a target, a tracking tool and a review schedule, kept in a shared tracker.

live.alt: The Crumb & Co. digital marketing strategy site for a fictional home bakery.

groups.title: AI and machine learning projects.
groups.sub: Each one runs on simulated data on an ordinary laptop, with no GPU, and turns a model’s output into a decision someone would act on. The figures are from each project’s own evaluation.

items.name: Autonomous Navigation System
items.desc: A complete self-driving robot stack in a 2D simulator: it sees, tracks, maps, plans a route and drives it, with a safety layer that can stop it.

notes.d: OpenCV perception and object tracking feed an occupancy map built from LiDAR and camera. A* or Dijkstra plans the route, and pure-pursuit control follows it.
Three planners on eleven maps reached the goal every time without a collision. A* found the same optimal path as Dijkstra while expanding 56% fewer nodes, and replans in about 19 ms.

items.name: Energy Demand Forecasting
items.desc: Forecasts a city zone’s hourly electricity demand a week ahead, then turns it into peak alerts and load-shifting plans.

notes.d: An R² of 0.95, with error 53% lower than a naive baseline forecast.
The forecast drives simulated procurement and load shifting, so the result is reported as money saved rather than only as model error.

items.name: Predictive Maintenance for IoT
items.desc: Predicts which machine will fail and why, from temperature, speed, torque and tool-wear sensors on simulated milling machines.

notes.d: The simulated data follows the structure of the UCI AI4I 2020 predictive-maintenance dataset, and the real dataset can be dropped in.
A virtual machine streams readings, and the model raises a maintenance alert before it breaks down.

items.name: AI Threat Detection
items.desc: A machine-learning intrusion detector for simulated network traffic, covering denial of service, port scans, brute force and data exfiltration.

notes.d: A Random Forest catches attack types it was trained on, while an Isolation Forest learns what normal traffic looks like and flags anything new.
Detections become security alerts mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and the whole pipeline runs in under a minute.

groups.title: Data analytics projects.
groups.sub: End-to-end pipelines: messy data in, cleaned, tested statistically, and out as a Streamlit dashboard and a written set of findings.

items.name: Climate Trend Analyzer
items.desc: 35 years of climate data for four Indian cities, tested for trends and forecast forward.

notes.d: Mann-Kendall tests find warming in all four cities, at 0.18 to 0.32 °C per decade, with Delhi fastest.
Z-score and Isolation Forest detection found 98% of injected heatwaves, and SARIMA forecasts the years ahead.

items.name: Retail Forecasting & Inventory
items.desc: Forecasts daily demand, then turns it into reorder points, safety stock and purchase orders.

notes.d: Models are judged on a 56-day recursive backtest against a seasonal baseline, on data that includes festivals, promotions and supplier delays.
In simulation, the new reorder policy cut stockout days from 6.7% to 2.2%.

items.name: Employee Performance Predictor
items.desc: Predicts whether an employee will be a low, medium or high performer, and suggests an HR action for each.

notes.d: Trained on 2,000 synthetic employees and scored on 400 it had never seen, with an F1 of 0.76.
Employees in the top quarter for training hours were predicted high performers 49% of the time, against 14% for the bottom quarter.

items.name: Poll Results Visualizer
items.desc: Turns raw poll and survey responses into vote shares, regional breakdowns and trends.

notes.d: Every share comes with a 95% margin of error, and the gap between leader and runner-up is tested for significance.
A dashboard filters by region, age, gender and date, and accepts your own CSV.

items.name: Expense Tracker Analytics
items.desc: Analyses a year of spending: category share, budget against actual, savings rate and unusual transactions.

notes.d: Bank data is private, so a seeded simulator reproduces real habits like rent, festive spending and weekend patterns, plus deliberate data-quality problems to clean.

items.name: Data Preprocessing Study
items.desc: Cleans and prepares the UCI Adult census dataset, and measures what each preprocessing choice actually changes.

notes.d: Fitting a target encoding before the train/test split inflated the test score by 0.026. Doing it after the split removes that false gain.

groups.title: Python automation and analysis tools.
groups.sub: Five Python tools that take messy input (an API, a CSV, a folder of resumes) and turn it into a decision, an alert or a report. Each one runs offline on sample data.

items.name: Automated Resume Screening
items.desc: Reads PDF, DOCX and TXT resumes, matches each against a job description, scores it out of 100 and sorts candidates into shortlisted, on hold or rejected.

notes.d: sklearn counts as scikit-learn and MySQL as SQL, and must-have skills weigh more than nice-to-haves.
A candidate is shortlisted only with a score of 65 or more and at least 60% of the must-have skills, and every result comes with a written reason. All sample resumes are synthetic.

items.name: Weather Forecast & Alerts
items.desc: Fetches current weather and a 5-day forecast for any city, summarises it with pandas and raises HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW alerts for rain, storms, heat, cold, humidity and wind.

notes.d: A simulation mode produces API-identical data for eight sample cities, so the whole pipeline runs offline.
No internet, a bad key, an unknown city and rate limits each get their own message. Alert thresholds come from .env or command-line flags.

items.name: Stock Market Data Analyzer
items.desc: Takes a ticker and a date range, cleans the price history and measures return, trend and risk, then saves seven charts and a plain-English report.

notes.d: Annualised volatility, maximum drawdown, Sharpe ratio and 95% value at risk, alongside 20, 50 and 200-day moving averages and crossover signals.
Prices come from Yahoo Finance, with a cached or bundled CSV as the fallback. Educational only, not financial advice.

items.name: Personal Expense Tracker
items.desc: Turns six months of messy expense records into clean data, budget alerts, six charts and a plain-English report.

notes.d: Duplicates, inconsistent categories, N/A, negative and missing amounts and bad dates are all fixed, and every fix is counted.
Where the money goes, month-on-month change, UPI vs card vs cash, weekday vs weekend, budget vs actual and savings rate.

items.name: Email Reminder System
items.desc: Reads contacts and reminders from CSV, fills personalised templates and sends each reminder when it falls due, logging every success and failure.

notes.d: Dry-run mode saves each email as an .eml preview instead of sending it, and SMTP credentials live in environment variables, never in code.

notes.t: One bad row doesn't stop the batch
notes.d: Invalid addresses and unknown contacts are marked FAILED and reported while the rest of the run carries on.

groups.title: Security, from the defending side.
groups.sub: ScamShield runs on a phone. The other five are dashboards that run on synthetic data or your own answers, and none of them scans, scrapes or contacts anything real. None is hosted, so here is what each one does.

items.name: ScamShield
items.desc: Screens incoming SMS and chat notifications for Indian scam patterns entirely on the phone, and explains each warning in English or Hindi.

notes.d: The manifest strips INTERNET with a merger directive, so permissions that bundled libraries add are removed. Nothing about a message can leave the device.
Nineteen weighted rules built from forty-four regexes across English, romanised Hinglish and Devanagari. One is negation-aware, so “never share this OTP” stays quiet.
Nine character substitutions are applied before matching a host against twenty-five real brand domains; UPI IDs are checked against a fifty-seven entry allowlist of genuine PSP handles.
An optional on-device language model rewrites the warning in plain words and can raise a verdict, never lower one. The rules stay in charge.

items.name: Phishing Detector
items.desc: Paste an email and it scores how likely it is to be phishing, then lists exactly why.

notes.d: A rule engine flags credential requests, urgency, lookalike senders and suspicious links, and an optional model adds a probability. The final score blends them 60/40, so the rules still drive it.
The analyser makes no network requests at all, and URLs are shown defanged, like hxxp://198[.]51…, so nothing on screen is clickable.

items.name: Password Analyzer
items.desc: Scores a password the way attackers actually guess, and says what to change.

notes.d: There is no password column anywhere, not even a hash, because people type real passwords into checkers. Only the score and length are kept, and a test proves the column does not exist.
It shows the textbook length × log₂(alphabet) figure beside a pattern-adjusted one, so you can see why Password123! scores high on the formula and falls to a guess list.

items.name: Social Media Privacy Risk
items.desc: A questionnaire about your own settings and habits that scores how exposed you are across ten areas.

notes.t: It never asks for the secret
notes.d: It asks whether your phone number is public, never what the number is. It does not scrape or track anyone.

notes.t: See what fixing it would do
notes.d: A what-if simulator re-scores you with improved settings, so you can see how much each change would lower the risk before you make it.

items.name: Threat Intelligence Dashboard
items.desc: Validates, enriches, scores and correlates threat indicators, and teaches people to recognise the same threats.

notes.d: How dangerous an indicator is and how sure we are of it get different scores, with sources graded A to F for reliability. A match is not reported as a confirmed breach.
Observed behaviours map to named MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and indicators are only checked for syntax: none is ever visited, resolved or contacted.

items.name: Network Intrusion Detection
items.desc: A simulated intrusion detection system: it generates synthetic traffic, detects attacks in it, and gives a security analyst a dashboard of scored, grouped incidents. It never captures real packets.

notes.t: Three ways to catch an attack
notes.d: Signature rules catch known patterns, a statistical model flags traffic that drifts from a learned baseline, and an optional Random Forest adds a third opinion. All three feed one risk score.
Alerts about the same activity within a time window are merged into one incident, and the dashboard reports how much that cut the alert count.

groups.title: Five services, one architecture.
groups.sub: Each is a FastAPI API with a React front end, tested in CI, and its database moves from SQLite to managed Postgres by changing one environment variable. The three that store files do the same from a local folder to an S3-compatible bucket. None is hosted, so here is what each one does differently.

items.name: Seatline
items.desc: Event planning with live RSVPs. Organisers publish; attendees answer going, maybe or not going, and every open dashboard updates without a refresh.

notes.t: It cannot oversell the last seat
notes.d: A seat is taken with one conditional UPDATE that only succeeds while the going count is below capacity. The loser of a race changes no rows and joins the waitlist, and a CHECK constraint enforces the same rule inside the database.
The suite releases thirty users on a thread barrier at the same instant, against PostgreSQL in CI, and asserts that exactly the capacity get in.

items.name: Smart Plant Care
items.desc: Virtual sensors, or an optional ESP32, report soil moisture, temperature, humidity and light. The cloud decides when to water and sends the pump command back to the device.

notes.d: The engine stops the pump at a maximum run time to prevent overwatering and enforces a cooldown between waterings, with thresholds set per plant profile.
A simulator stands in for the sensors and pump, and real ESP32 firmware sits in the same repository. A device that stops reporting is marked offline and raises an alert.

items.name: Assignment Portal
items.desc: Teachers publish assignments, students upload their work, and teachers return marks and written feedback.

notes.d: Submissions go to a private bucket and are only reached through signed links that expire after five minutes.

notes.t: The server decides what is late
notes.d: Lateness is stamped at submission time and kept after grading, so the timestamp is not something to argue about. The same app also runs on AWS Lambda through Mangum.

items.name: Hobby & Skills Tracker
items.desc: Log practice across hobbies, set goals, and share progress on a community feed with likes, comments and follows.

notes.d: Files are validated by their first bytes rather than their extension, and served through signed links that expire.
Likes, reports and new posts carry database uniqueness constraints, so a repeated request cannot create a second row.

items.name: Personal Diet Planner
items.desc: Builds a personal meal plan from a user’s profile and stores the plans and files in the cloud. Plans are general-wellness examples, not medical advice.

notes.d: A rule-based engine that needs no internet, API key or GPU generates plans on its own and takes over whenever the optional language model is unavailable. Each plan records which one produced it and why it fell back.

The 297 backend tests run on Python 3.11 and 3.13 against SQLite, and again against PostgreSQL, at 97% coverage, alongside 31 front-end tests, an end-to-end smoke run, and the full stack started from its Docker image.

about_text: About I started on microcontrollers, where you cannot attach a debugger to a bin on a street corner. So I learned to write the deciding part on its own and prove it before it ships. That is the thread through everything here. The settlement solver in SplitUPI is checked against a brute-force search. The token-rotation logic in Credential is driven through a real replay attack in its tests. The bin’s firmware has an in-browser twin so the same assertions run without the hardware. Moving to the web did not change the habit, it just changed the language. I am looking for full-stack or backend work, and I am equally happy on the side of a product that talks to hardware. Greenve I’m also building Greenve, a startup idea, with Reddi Malli Nandini and Rohit Singh. The Smart Dustbin comes under it: a bin that opens without being touched and tells the city when it needs emptying.

about.big: I started on microcontrollers, where you cannot attach a debugger to a bin on a street corner. So I learned to write the deciding part on its own and prove it before it ships.
cols: That is the thread through everything here. The settlement solver in SplitUPI is checked against a brute-force search. The token-rotation logic in Credential is driven through a real replay attack in its tests. The bin’s firmware has an in-browser twin so the same assertions run without the hardware.
Moving to the web did not change the habit, it just changed the language. I am looking for full-stack or backend work, and I am equally happy on the side of a product that talks to hardware.
about.note: I’m also building Greenve, a startup idea, with Reddi Malli Nandini and Rohit Singh. The Smart Dustbin comes under it: a bin that opens without being touched and tells the city when it needs emptying.

Supervised machine learning: regression and classification with Linear and Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forest and KNN, compared on a held-out test set and 5-fold cross-validation.
